title: Solve An Entry Threat Without Believing The Announcement Too Early
problem: A small company can enter a local delivery market. The incumbent says it will slash prices if entry happens. Fighting would hurt both firms, but accommodation would leave the incumbent with a smaller yet positive profit.
ordinary_setup: The first temptation is to treat the announcement as a fact about the future. The better first step is to separate what was said before entry from what the incumbent would want after entry has already occurred.
model_choice: Use an extensive-form game because time matters. The entrant chooses enter or stay out; if entry occurs, the incumbent chooses fight or accommodate. The model must preserve that later decision point instead of flattening the threat into a payoff-table label.
worked_solution: Solve the last decision first. At the incumbent's later node, compare fight with accommodate after entry is already sunk. If accommodation gives the incumbent 2 and fighting gives -1, accommodation is the later best response. Then move back to the entrant's choice. If entry followed by accommodation gives the entrant a positive payoff, entry survives the threat. The announcement was strategically relevant as a message, but it was not credible inside the solved tree.
math_check: Backward induction is the mathematical move. It says: choose the best action at the final decision point, replace that whole continuation with its payoff, then solve the earlier decision using that replacement. The important relation is not a fancy formula; it is the order of comparison.
assumption_audit: Check whether the incumbent truly gets another choice after entry, whether fighting is costly as described, and whether the entrant observes the same payoff logic. If fighting creates a reputation benefit in other markets, the payoff table is missing a later reward and the solution can change.
common_wrong_answer: The common wrong answer says the entrant should stay out because the incumbent threatened a price war. That answer confuses a spoken plan with a credible future action and skips the later incentive check.
transfer_rule: Whenever a new paper or business story uses a threat, first ask when the threatened action would be taken. If the threatened action is not optimal at that later moment, the model should not treat the threat as a hard constraint.

title: Delete A Product Feature Only After Every Rival Case Has Been Checked
problem: A platform can keep or remove a costly feature. Keeping the feature helps if a rival launches a premium product, but hurts if the rival stays basic. A manager wants to remove the feature because it looks expensive in the most likely case.
ordinary_setup: This is a pruning problem, not a prediction problem. The question is not which rival action seems likely. The question is whether one action is worse no matter what the rival does.
model_choice: Use a strategic-form table because the actions are chosen without modeling a later response. Put platform actions on one side, rival actions on the other, and compare the platform's payoffs row by row against every possible rival action.
worked_solution: Do not delete the feature if there is any rival action where keeping it does better. Suppose removing gives payoff 4 when the rival stays basic and 1 when the rival goes premium. Keeping gives payoff 2 when the rival stays basic and 5 when the rival goes premium. Removing looks better in the basic case, but keeping wins in the premium case. Neither action dominates the other. To choose between them, the model needs beliefs or a different solution concept.
math_check: Dominance uses a universal comparison: action A dominates action B only if A gives at least as much payoff against every rival action and strictly more in at least one case. The word every is doing the mathematical work.
assumption_audit: Check that the action list is complete and that the payoff entries really represent the platform's objective. If the premium rival action was accidentally omitted, deletion could look valid only because the table hid the case that protects the feature.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer deletes the feature because one case has the highest probability. That is expected-utility reasoning, not dominance. It may be a reasonable later calculation, but it is not a dominance deletion.
transfer_rule: When reading a model that removes actions before solving, look for the universal comparison. If the author only says an action is unlikely to pay off, they have not proved dominance.

title: Choose Random Inspection Probabilities By Making The Attacker Indifferent
problem: A security team can inspect morning or evening. An attacker can attack morning or evening. If the attacker guesses an uninspected time, the attacker gains; if inspection meets attack, the attacker loses.
ordinary_setup: The everyday problem is predictability. A fixed inspection time may be easy to explain inside the organization, but it gives the attacker a target. The security team needs randomness because the opponent is adapting to the pattern.
model_choice: Use a mixed-strategy game. Security chooses a probability of morning inspection; the attacker chooses a probability of morning attack. The point is not that either side feels uncertain. The point is that each side may deliberately prevent the other from exploiting a known pure action.
worked_solution: Let security inspect morning with probability p. The attacker compares attacking morning with attacking evening. If attacking morning is much better, the attacker will always attack morning; if attacking evening is much better, the attacker will switch. Security chooses p so those two expected payoffs are equal, leaving no obvious attack time. Then the attacker's mixing probability is found from the security team's comparison between inspecting morning and evening.
math_check: The key equation has the form expected payoff from morning attack equals expected payoff from evening attack. Each side's probability appears in the other side's comparison because mixing is chosen to discipline the opponent's best response.
assumption_audit: Check whether the attacker can observe or learn patterns, whether both attack times are genuinely available, and whether the loss numbers are stable. If the attacker cannot learn the pattern, a pure schedule may be fine. If there are hidden attack times, the equalization solved the wrong action set.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer picks fifty-fifty automatically. Equal probability is only correct in symmetric payoffs. When morning and evening have different stakes, the probability must be calculated from expected payoffs.
transfer_rule: When a paper uses randomization, ask whose incentive is being shaped. In strategic settings, probabilities are often chosen so the other side has no profitable predictable response.

title: Test Whether Future Punishment Can Hold A High-Price Path Together
problem: Two sellers have kept prices high for months. Either seller can secretly cut price today and win extra customers, but if cheating is discovered the other seller will cut prices in every later period.
ordinary_setup: The problem exists because today's temptation is close and concrete while tomorrow's punishment is delayed. Repetition matters only if future losses are heavy enough to change today's choice.
model_choice: Use an infinitely repeated game with a proposed cooperative path and a punishment path. Name the cooperative payoff, the one-time cheating payoff, the punishment payoff, and the discount factor that measures how much future payoffs count today.
worked_solution: Compare cooperating forever with cheating once and then being punished. If cooperation gives 6 each period, cheating gives 10 today, and punishment gives 2 afterward, cooperation survives when 6 plus the discounted future value of more 6s is at least 10 plus the discounted future value of 2s. A patient seller can prefer the cooperative path because losing the future stream is worse than the one-time gain.
math_check: The mathematical object is an incentive constraint. In words: value of staying on the path must be at least value of deviating today plus punishment tomorrow. The discount factor multiplies future terms, so a higher discount factor makes future punishment more powerful.
assumption_audit: Check monitoring, punishment credibility, and the length of the relationship. If cheating cannot be detected, punishment cannot target the deviator. If the game has a known final period, backward induction can unravel cooperation.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer says repeated interaction automatically creates cooperation. The course logic is stricter: repetition supplies a possible future cost, but the incentive inequality still has to pass.
transfer_rule: When a model claims cooperation is sustained by the future, find the one-shot deviation and the continuation loss. Without those two numbers, the claim is only a story about patience.

title: Decide Whether A Warranty Is A Signal Or Just Advertising
problem: A seller can offer a warranty on a used device. High-quality sellers expect few repairs. Low-quality sellers expect many repairs. Buyers see the warranty but not the true device quality.
ordinary_setup: The problem exists because buyers cannot directly see the hidden type. A warranty can help only if the action is cheaper or more valuable for one type than another; otherwise every type can copy it.
model_choice: Use a signaling game with types, actions, buyer beliefs, and prices. The seller type is private information, the warranty is an observed action, and the buyer's willingness to pay depends on what the action says about type.
worked_solution: Suppose a warranty raises the sale price by 5. A high-quality seller expects repair cost 1, so the warranty adds net value 4. A low-quality seller expects repair cost 8, so the same warranty loses net value 3. Then offering the warranty can separate high quality from low quality. Buyers can rationally believe warranty means high quality only because low-quality imitation is unattractive.
math_check: The mathematical move is an incentive-compatibility check plus belief updating. Each type must prefer the action assigned to it, and buyers' beliefs after seeing the action must match the behavior predicted by the model.
assumption_audit: Check whether repair costs really differ by type, whether buyers observe the warranty, and whether the price premium is large enough for good sellers but not bad sellers. If warranties are cheap for everyone, the signal collapses.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer says the warranty proves quality because it sounds reassuring. Game theory asks why a bad seller would not make the same reassuring promise if buyers rewarded it.
transfer_rule: When a paper calls something a signal, look for a separating cost or benefit. If all types can mimic cheaply, the action may still advertise, but it does not reveal hidden type by itself.

title: Separate Winning, Paying, And Value In An Ad Auction Rule
problem: An ad platform ranks ads by bid times predicted quality. A bidder asks whether raising its bid is profitable when the higher bid may improve rank but also changes payment if the ad wins.
ordinary_setup: The everyday problem is that one action changes several things at once. A higher bid can increase the chance of getting shown, alter the price paid, and interact with quality. Treating the winning bid as the whole story hides the mechanism.
model_choice: Use an auction model with private value, allocation rule, payment rule, and expected payoff. The bidder does not only compare prices; it compares value from clicks minus expected payment under each possible bid.
worked_solution: Break the bid change into pieces. First ask how the bid changes rank or probability of winning. Second ask what payment is made if the ad wins. Third multiply by the value of clicks or impressions. A bid is attractive only if the extra expected value from better allocation exceeds the extra expected payment and any quality tradeoff.
math_check: The expected payoff has the shape: chance of winning times value if winning minus chance of paying times payment if winning. Each term must be read separately because auction rules can change probability and payment in different directions.
assumption_audit: Check whether bidders know their values, whether quality scores are fixed or strategically changeable, and whether the payment rule is first-price, second-price, or generalized. Revenue-equivalence conclusions require a narrow environment, not just the word auction.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer says the highest bid always wins and pays that bid. That misses quality weighting, allocation probability, and payment rules, which are exactly the design levers in ad auctions.
transfer_rule: When reading a mechanism paper, translate the rule into allocation and payment before judging incentives. Rules are not labels; they are machines that turn private values and actions into consequences.

title: Decide Whether A Warning Changes Beliefs Or Only Creates Noise
problem: A project lead privately knows whether a launch is risky. The lead sends a message saying delay is wise. Engineers must decide whether the message should change their launch decision.
ordinary_setup: The problem exists because words can be cheap. A message can carry information only if the speaker's incentives make some messages more likely in some states than others.
model_choice: Use an information game with hidden state, sender incentives, receiver beliefs, and receiver action. The message is not automatically evidence; it becomes evidence only through the link between state, incentives, and speech.
worked_solution: Ask what the lead would say when launch is safe and what the lead would say when launch is risky. If the lead always wants delay because delay avoids blame, then the same warning appears in both states and carries little information. If the lead wants launch when safe and delay when risky, then the message can separate states and rationally move engineers' beliefs. The receiver's job is therefore not to judge whether the sentence sounds serious; it is to compare the sender's incentives across hidden states.
math_check: The mathematical move is belief updating over messages. The receiver asks: how likely is this message in each state? A message shifts beliefs only when those likelihoods differ for strategic reasons.
assumption_audit: Check sender incentives, message observability, and whether lying or exaggerating is costly. If the message is public, common-knowledge effects may matter too; if it is private, coordination may still fail even when the content is believed.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer treats all warnings as truthful information or all cheap talk as useless. The course distinction is sharper: cheap talk can matter, but only through incentives and beliefs.
transfer_rule: When a model includes communication, ask what the sender would say in every state. The informational content of a message is the pattern of incentives behind it, not the surface sentence, so communication has to be read as behavior chosen under incentives.

title: Explain Why Public Confirmation Matters After Everyone Privately Heard The Rumor
problem: Every trader has privately heard that a policy change is coming, but no trader knows whether the others heard it. Later, the regulator publicly announces the same policy change.
ordinary_setup: The factual content may be old for each individual, but the public event changes what everyone can assume about everyone else. Strategic action depends on other people's expectations, not only on private facts.
model_choice: Use a common-knowledge model rather than a simple private-information update. Track the fact, who knows the fact, who knows that others know, and whether that recursive awareness is shared enough to coordinate action.
worked_solution: Before the announcement, a trader may hesitate because selling is costly if others do not also sell. After the public announcement, each trader knows the others heard it and knows that the others can reason from the same public event. The same policy fact can therefore support a different equilibrium behavior because the belief hierarchy changed. The announcement works like a shared starting line: it gives everyone a reason to expect that everyone else is solving from the same premise.
math_check: The mathematical move is knowledge recursion. The relation is not just probability of the policy change; it is layers of belief about other players' beliefs. Common knowledge compresses those layers into a public event that everyone can use.
assumption_audit: Check that the announcement was public, that the audience understood it similarly, and that coordinated action is actually payoff-relevant. If the announcement is ambiguous or seen by only some traders, the common-knowledge conclusion is too strong.
common_wrong_answer: The wrong answer says the announcement adds nothing because everyone already knew the policy. That treats information as private facts only and misses the strategic role of shared awareness.
transfer_rule: When a paper says a public signal matters, ask whether the mechanism is new facts, shared interpretation, or higher-order belief. Those are different reasons for behavior to change, and confusing them makes private information look stronger than it is.
